items.content:
There are two ways AI progress could go very badly and that we must avoid.

First, we could lose control of the future to AI. This is unacceptable; we are unapologetically on Team Humanity, and AI must always serve people. To ensure that, we need ways to ensure that alignment and safety techniques stay ahead of progress in model capabilities.

Second, we could end up in a world with too much concentration of power. If an extraordinarily powerful AI is used by one person or company to impress their worldview onto everyone else, the results could be extremely dystopian.

Avoiding these two threats requires walking a narrow middle path; for example, one country could gain too much power. Another example is one lab ending up with too much power.
items.author: @sama

items.title: The world deserves confidence that American companies developing increasingly capable AI will act responsibly, especiall
items.content:
The world deserves confidence that American companies developing increasingly capable AI will act responsibly, especially as the trajectory of progress has steepened. Every frontier lab must deliver on this, and there is no reason any of us should come to work if we cannot.

We welcome a federal framework that sets consistent safety requirements for frontier AI. But we do not believe we need to wait for an anti-trust exemption or legislation to begin the work of providing this confidence. Consistent rules to manage frontier risk so that we can maximize the benefits are a good idea (and we are excited by ideas like independent auditors).

Years ago, companies like ours developed things like Responsible Scaling Policies and Preparedness Frameworks. Those were good for that moment, and focused primarily on the deployment of completed models, not what happens during their development process.

Today's shift to focusing on safe development and evaluation will need new tools. For example, at OpenAI we now formulate explicit safety cases in advance of frontier reinforcement learning runs we expect to significantly increase capability, in addition to the safety work we have long done in advance of model releases.

We hope that other companies will learn from our approaches and propose their own; we think shared standards for misalignment, monitoring, and safety will lead to better outcomes. We look forward to collaborating with our colleagues across the industry to formulate the best version of these.

When we talk about “pacing”, we do not mean “stopping”. Progress has been rapid and will continue to be. But it should be slower than it otherwise could be; interventions like safety cases and monitoring have significant costs.

Pacing will be well worth this cost; no amount of American competitive pressure should justify recklessness, or let capabilities get ahead of alignment and monitoring.

Where we will need the help of our government is for international coordination. But first we should do what we can ourselves.

Today, we're sharing three measurements that help track AI development:

2. How well AI agents are overseen.
3. How compute is allocated.

We provide a snapshot of these metrics from inside Anthropic. Any frontier developer could publish the same measures, and third parties could verify them.

memory has been a hot topic for the past ~2 years

every time we bring it up or do anything there, gets ton of interest,
items.content:
memory has been a hot topic for the past ~2 years

every time we bring it up or do anything there, gets ton of interest, but nothing sticks

few takes on why below:

- how to update and then use memory needs to be pretty tightly integrated with the harness. so its hard to build a standalone memory product

- the hardest part of memory is the logic of deciding what to remember. storing and even querying memory is not necessarily hard. the logic of deciding what to remember is often (a) application specific, (b) just prompting, which makes it hard to productize

- memory is not that useful in a general purpose agent, but more for when you are doing repeated tasks. more high usage ai agent are not just doing the same task repeatedly

- memory hasnt really proven to be useful for coding agents, and most agent things that take off happen first in coding agents

items.title: To the people quitting their jobs and making proclamations of AI concerns, here is what you should ACTUALLY be sharing i
items.content:
To the people quitting their jobs and making proclamations of AI concerns, here is what you should ACTUALLY be sharing in your tweet. 

⬇️ 

- how long you have worked in AI
- of that time, how long you have been worried (and specifically about what? Misalignment? Bioweapons? International coordination?)
- your magnitude of worry and why (including timelines, confidence scores, assumptions you’re tracking)
- actual specific things that can go wrong (“kill us all” is the most vague panic-inducing option you have; your previous employer would not have hired you if that was your answer on AI risk examples - pretend you are getting interviewed because Anderson Cooper likely will do it anyways), you can hedge, you can say “and that’s just what we can imagine today” or “and that’s just with the next model family” but say a real thing that non-AI-pilled-superusers can actually picture 
- you need specific things you are calling for. Real action. A literal meeting is not enough. Your AI risk mitigation suggestion against “AI killing us all” needs to be more impressive than a parent-teacher meeting. Again, you are smarter than your current tweets and you are wasting your opportunity to drive change just like Hinton when he left Google. Examples include: environmental standards at data centers (air pollution, water quality), third party evaluators in labs, increased federal investment in open source, verifiable criteria to join early testing groups, whistleblower protections, required public risk disclosures before model releases, 3x minimum increase in federal renewables investment to catch up to China’s per capita spend, block chip exports to non-allies, highlight companies doing great AI safety work that more people should support, literally anything other than just “guys idk we gotta meet or something” 
- have a non-engineer review it
- have a person not in tech review it 
- have someone outside of your generation review it 
- have at least one AI optimist review it 
- and this one may sound odd but I think you should read one war-time presidential speech before it 

You have an opportunity to do something deeply meaningful on your way out. That is more likely than not one of the reasons you joined your company in the first place. Tweeting vagueties and inciting panic contributes the opposite.

items.content:
An agent matched human decisions 94% of the time.

The 6% is the interesting part.

A customer of ours has around 150,000 employees and a policy that lets teams request discounts. Marketing wants one for an event. Sales wants one to close a deal.

The volume got so large globally that they had a dedicated team whose entire job was approving or denying those requests.

Before trusting agents with it, they ran a backwards test. Last 30 days, what would the agent have approved or denied?

94% match with what the humans actually did.

Their reaction was not let us automate everything. It was: if we can find the other 6% and route it to a person, we can roll this out.

They now spend about 3% of the time they used to spend on it.

items.content:
How to duplicate yourself in Claude (and stop explaining things twice):

1. Open Claude Cowork

Download the Claude desktop app.
Create a “Brain” folder on your computer and give Cowork access to it.

2. Record every meeting

I use Granola to capture every meeting notes. It joins the call in the background.

3. Connect it to Claude

Go to Settings → Connectors → Granola. Connect your account so Claude can read your notes.

4. Make a “Brain” folder

Use the folder you created in step 1 to keep your project notes together. Make sure Cowork has access to it.

5. Sort them by project

Create one folder per project. Ask Claude to organize the notes into that folder.

6. Use one template

Every note gets the same three parts:
> Decisions.
> Action items.
> Open questions.
Ask Claude to apply that structure to each meeting.

7. Ask Claude directly

“What did we decide on [project]?”. Claude can use your notes to answer. You don’t have to find the call and listen through it again.

8. Open Obsidian

Download Obsidian. It’s free. Open your “Brain” folder in it so you can read the saved notes yourself.

9. Keep it updated

After each meeting, ask Claude to add the new notes and organize them in the same folder. Open that folder in Obsidian to see the updates.

I never have to explain myself twice. Claude gets my meeting notes and knows what we agreed on and what I need to do next.

I could have made this much longer, but I won't. If you need help connecting apps to claude, go to: → https://t.co/TSAQqOpDeV

items.content:
I just cancelled my $200/mo claude subscription for this.

then spent a week rewriting every prompt and agents.md file i had, because i realized i'd built my entire setup around a problem astra doesn't actually have.

every rule i'd written over the past year assumed the model would run too far. ask before every action. read every doc before touching anything. stop after the first change and wait for review. that's the entire genre of agent-configuration advice, and i'd copied most of it religiously.

astra flips that completely. it doesn't run away. it stops, sometimes before the actual work is even done. the same rules i wrote to protect myself from a model that wandered off were now the exact thing blocking a model that finishes what it starts.

the fix, confirmed straight from openai's own team: make "can you..." mean "do it." finish the authorized work and prepare something reviewable before asking permission, instead of pausing at every single step. audit your agents.md and skill files directly too, since a vague or contradictory line in there is enough to make astra block itself or veer off in a way a looser model never would have.

the number that actually convinced me this wasn't just a vibe. on a honeypot test built to mimic a real security incident, the prior model reached targets it wasn't supposed to touch in 48.2% of runs. astra did it in 0%.

i also didn't know until this week that multi-agent orchestration is a real, documented feature sitting in astra's own official docs, alongside computer use and persisted reasoning, not a workaround someone hacked together. reasoning effort can change mid-conversation too, without losing your cache, on the standard model specifically.

i spent a week rewriting rules i'd trusted for a year, because the model they were written for doesn't exist anymore.

items.title: Launch HN: Skillsync (YC W26) – AI chat sessions made portable across agents
items.content:
Launch HN: Skillsync (YC W26) – AI chat sessions made portable across agents Hey HN, we're Nars & Nishant, founders of Skillsync (https://skillsync.com)

Skillsync lets you move your AI chats across every coding agent. Most of our work exists as conversations, which are currently scattered across our agents. Though stored locally, these conversations use different formats. This is annoying because you cannot simply switch between agents without starting over. We get locked into a single provider and their agent as we invest in skills and memories over time. Skillsync acts as a universal converter. It moves the entire session, including all the messages, reasoning and tool calls so you can pick up right where you left off.

Skillsync collects all your sessions in one place and makes them searchable. It breaks down what each session is carrying, including which loaded skills the agent is actually using, making stale context easy to spot. You can also create shared workspaces to sync sessions across your team. You can build your own closed loop systems. Everything runs locally except when you share to workspaces.

The core is an open-source Rust engine called txcript (https://github.com/skillsynchq/txcript). It translates a session from one agent's on-disk format into another's, mapping conversation, reasoning, and tool history. Think ffmpeg or pandoc, but for agent sessions.

On top of that engine is a local-first desktop app. Your agent sessions are normally scattered across different tools' folders in formats you'd never read by hand; the app surfaces them in one place with a UI that makes them actually readable, the conversation, the reasoning, and the tool calls, so you can revisit what happened, move a session into another agent, or share it with a teammate.

Skills and memory are stored as portable, human-readable markdown you own, and exposed to any agent over MCP for search and selective retrieval.

Sessions and translation run locally on your machine. The one thing that leaves is what you explicitly share into a team workspace.

It’s been surprising to us to see how locked-in people already are without realizing it. You don't notice you're trapped in one agent or harness until you try to leave, and by then you've got months of sessions stuck in a format only that tool can read. The lock-in is invisible right up until it's expensive.

Once sessions are portable, they stop being disposable logs and become something you can actually build on, spotting patterns in how you work, handing a session off to someone else, letting a non-technical teammate pick up where an engineer left off. The session turns out to be the unit of collaboration, and right now it's being thrown away.

Before Skillsync, Nars and I built an open-source payment orchestrator that let merchants route across many processors instead of getting locked into one (30k+ GitHub stars). Fighting vendor lock-in by making incompatible systems interoperate was the whole job. We came into YC with a different idea, but the more we lived inside coding agents the more we saw the same problem from the other side: your context is locked into whatever agent you start with, because every agent stores sessions differently and none of it moves.

Some of the things we’re seeing people do with Skillsync are:

- Moving a session between Claude Code, Codex, and Cursor mid-task, including when you hit a usage limit on one and want to keep going on another.

- Thinking through a problem in a browser Claude chat, then handing the whole thread to Claude Code or Codex to build.

- Sharing research sessions with a team. Everyone uploads their sessions, so teammates and their agents can build on each other's work instead of repeating it.

It's available as a Mac app, CLI and MCP. Here's the demo: https://youtu.be/7hVhSnSKGl8. Would love to hear your feedback and answer questions!

items.content:
My new favorite way to build with agents is to organize them into a factory.

This is the 4-step workflow:

1) Station. 
- A custom order gets its own station, so the order does not interfere with the rest of production. 
- In software, this station is a branch or a work tree.

2) Assembly line. 
- The agent writes code, changes files, and adds structure.

3) Quality control. 
- Does it turn on? 
- Does it fit? 
- Does it break under pressure? 
- In software, you run tests, open a preview, and read the logs and screenshots.

4) Shipping. 
- The product goes out the door. 
- You merge, deploy the PR, and write release notes.

If a product fails quality control, you send feedback to the product team.

Then you do the loop again.

Write each step of your agent workflow as a factory job.

I've got a thesis on where AI agents are heading.

Most people will read it as sci-fi. A few will get positioned early.

8 things I believe about the agentic economy:

1: Agents are going autonomous faster than the rails under them
> They can plan, pay and hire. They can't settle a disagreement.

2: Every agent-to-agent deal is a contract
> Every contract eventually produces a dispute.

3: Courts can't keep up
> A case takes months. An agent has already made  its next decision.

4: Smart contracts can't fix it alone
> They handle what code can check. "Did the work meet the brief?" isn't one of those.

5: Trusting one AI to judge is a security hole
> Prompt injection can talk a single model into the wrong answer.

6: The missing layer is adjudication
> Something neutral that rules in minutes.

7: Jobs shift toward judgement
> Agents do the work. You define what "done" means and decide who was right.

8: Whoever builds adjudication sits in the path of every agent deal
> EVERY DEAL

That's why I've been digging into GenLayer.

How it works:

> Intelligent Contracts read the web and understand plain English
> 5 random validators judge each outcome, each on a different model setup
> Majority agrees, it's accepted
> Appeal it and the panel grows to 11, 23, 47, up to around 1,000
> Common case: about 30 minutes

It’s a referee!

Randomness plus model diversity is the clever bit. An attacker can't know which models they need to fool.

So what’s already building on it: Internet Court, an open standard for agent-to-agent contracts with GenLayer as the disputes layer.

Testnet Bradbury is live. Mainnet is on the roadmap for Q4.

portal. genlayer. foundation

Yes… I am watching the plumbing more than the agents. The agents will be everywhere. The layer that decides who was right gets far less attention.

items.content:
I put in $250.

The bot turned it into +$13,000.

And I didn’t even build the thing from scratch.

I found an open-source project on GitHub, opened it in Claude Code, spent a couple of hours cleaning it up, understanding the logic, and making a few tweaks.

Then I hit Run.

Honestly, I expected it to blow the account in an hour.

So I minimized the terminal and went about my day.

That night, I checked back.

$250 → $600.

That’s when I started paying attention.

The strategy is surprisingly simple:

It trades 5-minute BTC marketsand waits until roughly the final 2 minutes.

By then, BTC has usually already made most of its move.

The bot looks for:

→ BTC moving roughly $70–$100
→ A clear directional trend
→ Contracts priced around $0.80–$0.99
→ Entries only in the direction of the move
→ Small hedges when the market becomes extremely imbalanced

If the direction holds until settlement, the contract pays $1.

The idea is basically:

Don’t predict the move.

Wait until the market has already revealed most of it.

Then trade the final stretch.

The code is public and available on GitHub:

[5-Min BTC Polymarket Bot](https://t.co/a4olIkytaR)

Free to inspect.

Just remember: past performance claims aren't proof the strategy will work going forward, and automated trading can lose money quickly.

If you want to understand how it works, read this before running anything. 👇

this is f*cking beyond comprehension.

Google engineers just shipped the entire agent lifecycle in one release: build, scale, govern. and every piece answers a specific way agents die in production

> context layers (Static, Turn, User, Cache): you decide what the model carries between turns, so token spend stops being a mystery

> Go joins Python and Java, with its own A2A SDK

then the part nobody builds for themselves:

> a dashboard on token consumption, latency, error rates and tool calls: the four things that actually kill an agent
> a traces tab that opens the real sequence of actions the agent took, step by step
> a playground wired to the deployed agent, past sessions included, so debugging is not a redeploy loop
> an Evaluation Layer with a User Simulator, because you cannot unit test a non deterministic system

and the part that decides whether it ever ships:

> agents get native identities as first class IAM principals: least privilege applies to them like it does to people
> Model Armor screens prompt injection, tool calls and responses, inline for Gemini or over REST
> Security Command Center inventories every agentic asset and flags data exfiltration by an agent

ADK is already at 7 million downloads. the runtime has a free tier, and express mode runs off a Gmail address.

Claude
items.content:
ran both Claude and GPT-6 Astra against DaVinci Resolve's native MCP server, here's what actually separates them

Claude + DaVinci:

- built a full project from scratch, imported media, synced dual-system audio, de-camed a film scan into individual shots
- assembled a 15-minute rough edit from raw footage, correctly reordering scenes to follow a process
- automated a 10-20 hour TIFF cache render + final H.265 export unattended, recovering from a Resolve crash mid-run
- generated 20 vertical cut-downs from a single horizontal timeline with smart reframe applied automatically, one unresolved gap issue due to an API limitation, not Claude's error
- workflow here is single-shot, heavily instructed step by step

GPT-6 Astra + DaVinci:

- paired with Gemini for actual visual scene understanding, not just transcription, so it can identify what's literally in frame (a whiteboard, a room, people) and auto-censor sensitive content it sees on screen
- run as a loop instead of a single instruction: given one large prompt with all source files, tools, and editing preferences, then left to work, review its own output, and revise autonomously until done
- produced 4 fully edited training videos end to end, b-roll, music, image generation, captions, in 1 hour 55 minutes
- token cost was dramatically lower in this workflow, 3% of weekly usage vs a much heavier spend on the code-based editing method used previously

the real fork isn't which agent is smarter, it's workflow shape

Claude's DaVinci demo is a single, tightly scoped session, best when you already know exactly what you want and want to direct it step by step

Astra's DaVinci demo is a loop with Gemini bolted on for vision, best when you want to hand off a full batch of raw footage and voiceovers and come back later to a finished draft

both are still assistant editors, not replacements, procedural work (syncing, organizing, rough cuts, rendering) is what's actually being automated here, the creative judgment on what makes a good cut still needs a human pass

Huge hack if you build Claude skills for clients:

Don't spend the whole call watching them click through a process. Have them record a Loom before the call.

-Client records one Loom walking through the process
-Download the video, upload it to Gemini
-Prompt: "Write a step-by-step SOP of this process as a Google Doc, formatted so Claude can turn it into a skill"
-Paste the SOP into Claude, run AOA (Audit, Optimize, Automate) on it, then say "turn this into a skill"

Clients will be impressed by all the effort they "think" you did before the call when all you really did was upload a video and copy/paste one prompt.

I believe Claude can watch video now but for a while Gemini was the only LLM that could do this well (if at all).

How to use Jev, and where it actually gives you the 100x:

setup takes 10 minutes:

1. join the waitlist, people are getting approved same day
🔗 https://t.co/uO7aescvbM

2. install the official skill so your agent writes correct calls:

- npx skills add typesafe-ai/skills --skill typesafe-ai

on Claude Code it's two commands, the marketplace add on its own doesn't install anything:

- claude plugin marketplace add typesafe-ai/skills
- claude plugin install typesafe@typesafe-ai

3. create an API key in the dashboard

4. in your prompt just say: "use the TypeSafe skill"

now the part nobody is posting:

the 100x isn't the model, it's where you put it

you don't get it by swapping your LLM for Jev
you get it by deleting the calls that never needed a language model

open your agent and find every call that just picks something:

> which tool next
> is this spam
> is this chunk relevant
> does this need a human
> is this diff risky

none of those are writing tasks
they're if statements you outsourced to a frontier model

here's the upgrade, in order:

1. replace each one with a typed question
Choice picks from up to 255 options, Score places it on a 2-10 level scale, Noul returns a raw 0-1

2. batch them
questions in one call run in parallel and barely move the latency, and output tokens are free
so ask every question you might need, including the ones you'll throw away

3. threshold on confidence, not on the answer
under 0.5 escalate to a big model or a human
0.85+ before anything irreversible

4. never let it invent options
build the candidate list in code, from the DOM, the retriever, the tool trace
then let it pick

5. put it in the loop, not next to it
router picks the cheap model, gate checks the tool call before it runs, judge verifies the output after
that's where the heaviest calls in your agent are hiding

6. start with compaction tonight
score every tool call, drop the dead ones, keep the survivors verbatim instead of a lossy summary
lowest effort win available and you'll see it on tomorrow's bill

the honest part:

text only right now, no images, no audio
and on broad benchmarks it loses to frontier models

but somebody ran 18,514 emails through it zero-shot and got 98.33%
against a TF-IDF classifier trained on 14,800 labelled examples that got 98.39%

no training data, $1.12 total

it wins on narrow, well specified decisions
which is most of what your agent is actually doing all day
